Forecasting Project Cash Flows

Estimating CFs: Initial Outlay

Initial Outlay: What is the cash flow at “time 0?”

Project Free Cash Flows=EBIT(1−T)+DEP−(CAPEX+ΔNOWC)\text{Project Free Cash Flows} = EBIT \left( 1 - T \right) + DEP - \left( CAPEX + \Delta NOWC \right)

=(Rev−Costs−Dep)(1−T)+DEP−CAPEX−ΔNOWC= \left( Rev - Costs - Dep \right) \left( 1 - T \right) + DEP - CAPEX - \Delta NOWC

What we are actually doing

  • No Revenue or costs typically at time 0
  • Only the Depreciation, CAPEX, and NOWC

(0−0−Dep)(1−T)+Dep−CAPEX−ΔNOWC\left( 0 - 0 - Dep \right) \left( 1 - T \right) + Dep - CAPEX - \Delta NOWC

−Dep+T*Dep+Dep−CAPEX−ΔNOWC-Dep + T \ast Dep + Dep - CAPEX - \Delta NOWC

T*Dep−CAPEX−ΔNOWC=−(CAPEX−t*Dep)−ΔNOWCT \ast Dep - CAPEX - \Delta NOWC = -\left( CAPEX - t \ast Dep \right) - \Delta NOWC

Alternative Steps (Book)

  • Find the CAPEX* at time 0
    • Cost - (T × Depreciation)
  • Then find any change in ΔNOWC
  • The sum of these is the FCF at time zero or the initial capital outlay

Estimating Incremental CFs

Project Free Cash Flows=EBIT(1−T)+DEP−(CAPEX+ΔNOWC)\text{Project Free Cash Flows} = EBIT \left( 1 - T \right) + DEP - \left( CAPEX + \Delta NOWC \right)

=(Rev−Costs−Dep)(1−T)+DEP−CAPEX−ΔNOWC= \left( Rev - Costs - Dep \right) \left( 1 - T \right) + DEP - CAPEX - \Delta NOWC

  • For each year we need to estimate our revenue and costs as well as any depreciation expense
  • For most of our problems there is 100% depreciation immediately

Estimating the Terminal Cash Flow

  • Salvage value
    • Book value is the initial price for the asset minus its total accumulated depreciation
    • Tax could be a credit

ATsalvage=Salvage Value−T(Salvage Value−Book Value)AT_{salvage} = \text{Salvage Value} - T \left( \text{Salvage Value} - \text{Book Value} \right)

  • Recovery of any net operating working capital
    • Spare parts

Estimating the Terminal Cash Flow

Project Free Cash Flows=EBIT(1−T)+DEP−(CAPEX+ΔNOWC)\text{Project Free Cash Flows} = EBIT \left( 1 - T \right) + DEP - \left( CAPEX + \Delta NOWC \right)

=(Rev−Costs−Dep)(1−T)+DEP−CAPEX−ΔNOWC= \left( Rev - Costs - Dep \right) \left( 1 - T \right) + DEP - CAPEX - \Delta NOWC

  • Salvage value

ATsalvage=Salvage Value−T(Salvage Value−Book Value)AT_{salvage} = \text{Salvage Value} - T \left( \text{Salvage Value} - \text{Book Value} \right)

  • Assume that CAPEX decreases by this amount
  • Positive AT salvage value increases FCF
  • Negative AT salvage value decreases FCF
  • Recovery of any net operating working capital
    • Spare parts
    • ΔNOWC

Issues with Estimating Cash Flows

  • Sunk costs=exclude. Ask yourself if rejecting the project affects this cost.
  • Financing costs, such as interest expense=EXCLUDE. Already included in WACC.
  • Opportunity Costs=INCLUDE. Generally revenues forgone from using land or building for another purpose other than the project
  • Externalities=effects of a project on cash flows in other part of the firm. Can be positive or negative and should be INCLUDED as part of the project’s incremental cash flows.
  • Cannibalization=INCLUDE. A negative externality, occurs when the introduction of a new product diminishes the sales of existing products.

Replacement Projects

  • Assume old equipment is sold and new equipment is purchased.
  • Also relies on incremental free cash flows
    • Estimate free cash flows associated with new equipment
    • Deduct free cash flows associated with existing equipment
    • Use the difference (incremental free cash flows) to calculate net present value

Project Risk

Market risk is the most relevant risk for capital projects. However, it is very difficult to measure since there is no historical data on a proposed new project

Three ways to look at the risk of one project
Risk Type Characteristics
Stand-alone risk Measured by σ. Risk of single project company, single company stockholder
Corporate risk Considers firm’s other projects (i.e. diversification) and includes σ and correlation with firm’s other projects
Market risk Most relevant to a diversified investor. Measured by β

Risk Measurement and Correlation

Stand-alone risk is the easiest to measure and most often used in capital budgeting decisions.
While not theoretically correct, it does not necessarily lead to poor decisions.
Correlation between all risk types is high since projects tend to be focused on a firm’s core business and its corporate risk is likely to be highly correlated with its market risk.

Sensitivity Analysis

  • Sensitivity analysis measures the effect of changes in a single variable on a project’s NPV.
  • To perform a sensitivity analysis, all variables are fixed at their expected values, except for the variable in question which is allowed to fluctuate.
  • Resulting changes in NPV are noted.
  • Identifies variables that may have the greatest potential impact on profitability and allows management to focus on these variables.
  • Shows how sensitive NPV is to changes in one specific variable

Scenario Analysis

  • Like sensitivity analysis, only different in that:
    • More than one variable can be changed
    • Discrete probabilities applied to different outcomes
    • Looks at project specific volatility and standalone risk
  • Can be used to determine whether a company’s weighted average cost of capital (WACC) should be adjusted up or down for a specific project.
  • Without potentially adjusting the WACC, riskier projects would have higher NPV’s (since higher risk implies higher return) resulting in a failure to risk adjust or risk weight specific projects

Determining Expected NPV, Variance, σNPV, and CVNPV

E(NPV)=0.25(−$43.1)+0.5($10.4)+0.25($63.9)=$10.4E(NPV) = 0.25 \left( -\$43.1 \right) + 0.5 \left( \$10.4 \right) + 0.25 \left( \$63.9 \right) = \$10.4

σNPV2=[0.25(−$43.1−$10.4)2+0.5($10.4−$10.4)2+0.25($63.9−$10.4)2]\sigma_{NPV}^2 = \left[ 0.25 \left( -\$43.1 - \$10.4 \right)^2 + 0.5 \left( \$10.4 - \$10.4 \right)^2 + 0.25 \left( \$63.9 - \$10.4 \right)^2 \right]

σNPV=(σ2)12=$37.8\sigma_{NPV} = \left( \sigma^2 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \$37.8

CVNPV=$37.8/$10.4=3.6CV_{NPV} = \$37.8 / \$10.4 = 3.6

NPV Practice

  • A project pays $5k per year for 10 years and then $9k per year for the following ten years. The 20 year IRR is 8.52% and the WACC is 8%. What is the NPV?
  • First, what are we missing for NPV?
  • How can IRR help?
  • Use the cash flow register
    • 0 for CF0, 5k for 10 years, 9K for another 10 years.
    • Then use 8.52% for I and get NPV
  • Go back and update CF register and use WACC for I.

Replacement Discussion

  • A gas power plant was built 6 years ago at a cost of $120M with a useful life of 10 years. It is being depreciated to zero using 10-year straight-line depreciation. The plant can be sold today for $40M. This plant has no salvage value at the end of its life.
  • The nuclear plant would cost $500M to build today. It can be fully depreciated and expensed immediately. The Nuclear Fusion Plant is expected to have a salvage value of $50M at the end of the plant’s 4-year life. The nuclear plant will reduce OPEX by $150M each year increase revenues by $40M each year. The company’s marginal tax rate is 25%, and this project has a WACC of 11%.
  • What is the incremental initial cash flow for this replacement analysis?
  • What is the year 1 incremental CF for the proposed plant replacement?
  • What is the terminal end of project incremental cash flow at the end of year 4 for this replacement analysis?
